description: Composite monarchy (1162–1516) uniting the Crown of Aragon with the County of Barcelona and later Valencia, Sicily, Naples, and Sardinia; pioneered constitutional federalism through the Union of the Crown and the institution of the Justicia, while its Mediterranean empire made Barcelona and Valencia leading commercial powers before union with Castile.

lifecycle_phases.description: The union of the Kingdom of Aragon and County of Barcelona under Alfonso II (1162) creates the Crown of Aragon. The Aragonese-Catalan fleet becomes dominant in the western Mediterranean. James I 'the Conqueror' (1213–1276) captures Mallorca (1229) and Valencia (1238), completing the Iberian Reconquista in the east. The treaty of Corbeil (1258) ends Aragonese claims in southern France and French claims in Catalonia.

The Sicilian Vespers (1282), a spontaneous massacre of French Angevins in Sicily, leads to Peter III of Aragon's conquest of Sicily through his wife's Hohenstaufen claim. The resulting War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282–1302) lasts 20 years but ends with Aragonese Sicily recognized. The Catalan Company, Aragonese mercenaries, subsequently carves out the Duchy of Athens (1311).

Alfonso V 'the Magnanimous' (1416–1458) conquers Naples (1442), creating a Mediterranean empire including Sicily, Sardinia, and Naples. His death divides the inheritance: Castile gets the Iberian Aragon, Naples goes to a bastard line. Ferdinand II of Aragon's marriage to Isabella of Castile (1469) and their joint accession (1479) creates unified Spain, with Aragon contributing its Mediterranean empire.

rise_factors.description: The Catalan merchant marine and Barcelona's commercial networks dominated western Mediterranean trade; the Aragonese conquest of Majorca, Sardinia, and Sicily gave the Crown control of the key islands and ports of Mediterranean commerce

The almogavars, light Catalan-Aragonese infantry from the Reconquista frontier, were among the most effective soldiers in medieval Europe; the Catalan Company's mercenary campaigns demonstrated this force's lethality across the eastern Mediterranean
Aragonese navy dominated the western Mediterranean from the 13th century; control of Majorca, Sardinia, Sicily, and ports in Tunisia gave command of sea lanes critical for Italian trade

Strategic marriage policy and conquest extended Aragonese rule to Sicily (1282), Naples (1442), and briefly Athens; the Crown's composite nature allowed flexible administration of disparate territories

Barcelona and Valencia were among Europe's most commercially active cities; the Consell de Cent (city council) and merchant guilds provided sophisticated commercial law; Aragonese banking competed with Italian firms

Aragonese control of Sicily (1282), Sardinia (1323), Naples (1442), and trading posts in North Africa created a western Mediterranean commercial empire generating revenues that dwarfed any individual kingdom's resources.

The Aragonese Cortes and Justicia institution created one of medieval Europe's most sophisticated constitutional frameworks, limiting royal power and guaranteeing noble privileges, enabling stable governance across a multi-kingdom composite state.

decline_factors.description: Governing Sicily, Sardinia, Naples, Valencia, Catalonia, and Aragon simultaneously required constant military and diplomatic effort across three countries; the Aragonese-Catalan empire lacked the administrative depth to hold all its territories simultaneously

The Aragonese constitution (Fueros) gave nobles and Cortes extensive veto powers; the Justicia de Aragón could block royal decrees; governance required constant negotiation rather than executive command

Union with Castile under Ferdinand and Isabella subordinated Aragonese institutions to the larger partner; Castilian dominance in the Americas and the shift of trade routes to the Atlantic marginalized Barcelona's Mediterranean empire
